hook: Yoshua Bengio has spent his career pushing neural networks from a marginal idea into the foundation of modern AI, and more recently has turned much of his attention to the risks that AI now poses. Born in Paris and raised in Canada, he earned a PhD in computer science from McGill University before joining the Universite de Montreal, where he has been a professor since the early 1990s. His 2003 paper A Neural Probabilistic Language Model helped establish the use of learned word representations in language modeling, an idea that became central to later large language models, and in 2014 he co-authored the paper introducing generative adversarial networks with Ian Goodfellow and others. He founded Mila, the Quebec Artificial Intelligence Institute, building it into one of the world's largest academic centers for deep learning research, and in 2016 co-founded the AI startup Element AI. In 2018 he shared the ACM A.M. Turing Award with Yann LeCun and Geoffrey Hinton for his contributions to deep learning. In recent years he has chaired the International AI Safety Report and, in June 2025, launched LawZero, a nonprofit research organization focused on building safe, non-agentic AI systems.

standing.record: The records add up to a career in two halves. The first is technical: the 2003 paper A Neural Probabilistic Language Model, the 2014 paper introducing generative adversarial networks with Ian Goodfellow and others, and the 2016 textbook Deep Learning with Goodfellow and Aaron Courville. The second is institutional: Mila, which the site lists as founded in 1993, and Element AI, which the profile says he co-founded in 2016. The pattern running through them is a move from building the foundations of deep learning to addressing the risks it creates, through the International AI Safety Report and LawZero. The site carries no lawsuits naming him or his companies and no news stories about him, so the record is a profile and a single company entry rather than a litigation or coverage trail.
standing.standing: Yoshua Bengio stands in these records as a professor at the Universite de Montreal, the founder of Mila, the Quebec Artificial Intelligence Institute, and the founder of LawZero, a nonprofit launched in June 2025. The site lists Mila as a nonprofit in Montreal, Quebec, Canada, founded in 1993, and describes it as one of the world's largest academic centers for deep learning research. He shared the 2018 ACM A.M. Turing Award with Yann LeCun and Geoffrey Hinton, and he has chaired the International AI Safety Report. Beyond those entries, the records give no measure of his current holdings, funding or formal authority, so his standing here rests on institutions and honors rather than on any listed ownership or valuation. What he controls or influences, as the records show, is Mila as a research institution and LawZero as a new nonprofit.
